newsitem.title: UK: S&P assigns investment grade ratings to Egypt.
newsitem.headline: S&P assigns investment grade ratings to Egypt.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Wednesday it had assigned investment grade credit ratings to Egypt to reflect the country's accelerating structural reforms.
The rating agency assigned BBB minus long-term and A3 short-term foreign currency credit ratings.
It also gave A minus long-term and A2 short-term local currency credit ratings to the country, affecting around 34 billion Egyptian pounds ($10 billion) of senior unsecured treasury bills and bonds.
The outlook on the long-term ratings is stable, S&P said.
"Egypt's investment-grade ratings reflect a robust commitment to fiscal restraint," S&P said in a statement.
It reflected Cairo's reforms, including privatisation, trade liberalisation and deregulation and a deepening political consensus behind the reforms.
Egypt's external debt service, including short-term debt, equivalent to 17 percent of annual exports, is among the lowest of similarly rated nations, S&P said.
Fiscal deficits, at 1.3 percent of gross domestic product in fiscal 1994-95 and 1995-96 and targeted to fall to 1.1 percent in 1996-97, should remain modest for the rest of the decade.
"The higher local currency rating reflects Egypt's sound fiscal policies and the central bank's success in lowering inflation and real interest rates at moderate levels going forward," S&P said.

S&P said Egypt's ratings were constrained by low per capita income, at about $1,200 in 1997, and still weak social infrastructure that will continue to test the government's commitment to conservative financial policies.
A moderately high, although declining, net government debt burden estimated at 53 percent of GDP in fiscal in 1997 and a weak financial sector were also constraining factors, S&P said.
Low but improving levels of savings and investment and export earnings still concentrated in petroleum products, tourism and remittances were additional depressive factors.
